./.title: Introduction
./.body:
Introduction
This manual guides users through installing Eclipse Kura on a Raspberry Pi and
connecting it to Cloud Multiplatform H2Train through Eclipse Kapua for remote
device maintenance.
Purpose and Scope
The manual covers the prerequisites, installation, and connection settings used
in the project's current implementation. It provides commands, screenshots, and
reference material to support the configuration of a device for maintenance
operations, including application updates.
Intended Audience
The intended audience is project participants and technical staff responsible
for device setup. Readers should be familiar with basic Linux terminal commands,
network settings, and the use of sudo for administrative tasks.
Reading Guide
The manual is organized as follows:



Chapter
Content




1. System Overview
Components, architecture, communication, and access mechanisms.


2. Hardware, Software, and Prerequisites
Device requirements and VPN access.


3. Installing Eclipse Kura
Java and Kura installation and initial console access.


4. Connecting to Cloud Multiplatform H2Train with Eclipse Kapua
Registration and maintenance service configuration.


5. Glossary and Reference Material
Definitions, external documentation, and deployment resources.


6. Changelog
Revision history and contact details.



Read chapter 1 for the technical background, then follow chapters 2 through 4
in sequence. Consult chapter 5 as needed.
Use the navigation panel to move between chapters and sections. Run commands
on the Raspberry Pi unless the procedure specifies otherwise.

chapters/01-system-overview.html.title: 1. System Overview
chapters/01-system-overview.html.body:
1. System Overview
The H2Train system combines device-side services, a private network, and cloud
management services. This chapter explains their responsibilities, how messages
travel between them, and how access is controlled.
1.1 Main Components and Responsibilities



Component
Responsibility in this deployment




Raspberry Pi 4 Model B
Hosts the operating system, Java runtime, and Kura installation. It acts as the edge gateway.


Raspberry Pi OS
Provides the Linux environment, network interfaces, package-management tools, and administrative access needed to install and operate the software.


Eclipse Temurin JDK 17
Supplies the Java runtime used to execute Kura, together with Java development tools.


Eclipse Kura
Runs on the Raspberry Pi and provides the administration console, cloud connection services, and remote command execution service.


Eclipse Kapua
Provides the cloud environment used for user access, device communication, and maintenance management.


Tailscale
Provides the private network connectivity used to connect the device and the Kapua environment from different locations.


H2Train registration services
Provide the web forms used to request Tailscale access and create individual Kapua users.



Cloud Multiplatform H2Train is the project environment in which these components
are used together. The registration services support access provisioning;
ongoing device communication uses the configured broker connection.
1.2 Edge-to-Cloud Architecture
On the Raspberry Pi, Kura runs within the Java environment and uses the device's
Ethernet or Wi-Fi connection to reach the remote services. Its maintenance cloud
connection communicates with the MQTT broker using MQTT over TLS, identified by
the mqtts:// scheme in the broker URL.
The current implementation uses Tailscale to provide private connectivity across
different geographical locations. This network access must be established
before Kura can reach the configured broker. The broker address, account name,
and connection settings are specified in
chapter 4.
TLS provides certificate-based protection for the broker connection. The
certificate imported into Kura's SSLKeystore establishes the trust required
by the documented setup. VPN access and TLS configuration are therefore both
part of the connection procedure.
Browser-based administration provides access to the Kura console on the device
and the Kapua console on the server. The Kura console is used to configure local
services; the Kapua console provides the server-side administration view.
The planned cloud-hosted Kapua deployment will provide a server address reachable
from users' networks through DNS. Tailscale supplies the connectivity used by
the current implementation while that deployment is being prepared.
1.3 Data Flow and Device Management
Kura initiates the connection to the broker using the configured account,
credentials, and client ID. The broker routes messages according to their MQTT
topics and the permissions assigned to the connecting account. Communication
over this connection supports messages from the device and management requests
sent toward the device.
The maintenance connection is configured through three related Kura services:

CloudService-Maintainer: provides the cloud service instance used for
maintenance communication.
DataService-Maintainer: manages message delivery and enables automatic
connection at startup.
MqttDataTransport-Maintainer: defines the broker endpoint, account context,
authentication credentials, client ID, and MQTT connection settings.

The CommandService handles remote command execution on the Raspberry Pi.
Its configuration includes a command password, working directory, execution
timeout, and privilege setting. These settings prepare the device for the
maintenance operations described in the deployment.
1.4 Authentication and Access Control
The system uses separate credentials and permissions for network access, user
identity, broker communication, and remote commands.



Access mechanism
Role




Institutional email verification
Confirms access to an approved email address before the registration service issues a Tailscale auth key.


Tailscale auth key
Registers the device on the private network.


Individual Kapua account
Identifies a registered user with the role assigned by the registration system.


Maintenance broker credentials
Authenticate Kura's maintenance connection with the dedicated account and its assigned permissions.


Broker certificate trust
Allows Kura to validate the broker certificate using the certificate material imported into SSLKeystore.


Command password
Provides the password configured for remote command requests handled by CommandService.



The device's MQTT client ID identifies its connection and must be unique within
the account. The Tailscale device name and the Kapua username are configured
separately during their respective registration procedures.
Configuration details are provided in chapter 4.
Definitions and supporting documentation are available in
chapter 5.

chapters/02-requirements.html.title: 2. Hardware, Software, and Prerequisites
chapters/02-requirements.html.body:
2. Hardware, Software, and Prerequisites
This chapter defines the hardware and software prerequisites for installing
Eclipse Kura. It describes the equipment and operating environment used
successfully in the current implementation.
Devices with similar capabilities may also be suitable. However, their operating
system, processor architecture, and compatibility with the selected Kura package
must be checked before applying the installation procedure.
2.1 Hardware Requirements
The current implementation uses a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B with 4 GB of RAM.
The following table summarizes the specifications of the hardware used; it does
not define the minimum requirements for every Kura deployment.



Component
Specification




Processor
Broadcom BCM2711, quad-core Cortex-A72 (ARMv8), 64-bit SoC at 1.8 GHz


Memory
4 GB LPDDR4-3200 SDRAM in the model used


Wireless connectivity
2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz IEEE 802.11ac Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 5.0, and Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE)


Wired connectivity
Gigabit Ethernet


USB ports
Two USB 3.0 ports and two USB 2.0 ports


Display outputs
Two micro-HDMI ports, supporting up to 4K at 60 frames per second


Display interface
Two-lane MIPI DSI display port


Camera interface
Two-lane MIPI CSI camera port


Audio and composite video
Four-pole stereo audio and composite video port


Video processing
H.265 decoding at 4K/60 fps; H.264 decoding at 1080p/60 fps and encoding at 1080p/30 fps


Storage
microSD card slot for the operating system and data storage


USB-C power input
5 V DC, with a supply rated for at least 3 A


Alternative power input
5 V DC through the GPIO header, with a supply rated for at least 3 A



For further specifications, consult the
official Raspberry Pi 4 Model B product page.
Provide a microSD card for the operating system and a suitable power supply.
The USB-C and GPIO entries above describe alternative power inputs.
2.2 Peripherals and Network Connectivity
For local setup and interaction with the Raspberry Pi, a keyboard, mouse, and
display with a suitable micro-HDMI cable or adapter are recommended. Remote
administration through SSH is also possible once network access and SSH have
been configured.
Configure at least one network interface before starting the installation:

Ethernet: connect the device to the network using an Ethernet cable.
Wi-Fi: configure the wireless network and verify that the device can connect.

Internet access is required to update system packages and download Kura and its
dependencies.
2.3 Operating System
The current implementation uses Raspberry Pi OS based on Debian 13 (Trixie).
Raspberry Pi OS was previously known as Raspbian. Official images are available
from the Raspberry Pi OS download page.
Use the 64-bit edition for the procedure in
Chapter 3: Installing Eclipse Kura, which uses
the aarch64 installer. The Adoptium repository configured in that chapter also
targets the trixie release.
2.4 User Accounts and Administrative Permissions
The device must have a user account that can execute commands with administrative
privileges through sudo. These privileges are needed to install packages,
configure repositories, and restart the device.
Confirm that the account can use sudo before beginning the installation.
2.5 Software Requirements
This section covers system preparation and the temporary VPN setup required to
connect Eclipse Kura and Eclipse Kapua from different geographical locations.
2.5.1 Prepare the System
Update the package lists and upgrade installed system packages before installing
Kura. The commands are provided in section 3.1.
An existing Kura or Java installation is not required: Chapter 3 covers the
installation of Eclipse Temurin JDK 17, the required utilities, and Eclipse Kura
5.6.2. Ensure that wget is available before the installer download step in
section 3.2. For the current remote connectivity setup, also install and configure
Tailscale as described below.
2.5.2 Understand the Temporary VPN Setup
The planned deployment will host Eclipse Kapua on a cloud server with a DNS name
that resolves to an address reachable from users' networks. This solution is not
yet available in the current implementation.
Until that deployment is available, Tailscale provides a shared private network
between the Kura device and the Kapua server, allowing them to communicate from
different locations. Tailscale was selected for this temporary solution because
it offers a free tier for connecting multiple devices. 
To connect a device to the H2Train Tailscale network, first install Tailscale on
the device. Then request an auth key, verify your email address, and use the
issued key to join the network, following the steps below.
2.5.3 Install Tailscale
Install Tailscale on the Raspberry Pi before requesting an auth key. Open a
terminal on the device. If curl is not available, install it first with
sudo apt install -y curl.
Run the following command to download and execute the official Tailscale
installation script:
curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh | sh

For further installation details, consult the
official Tailscale Linux installation guide.
Once installation is complete, proceed to
section 2.5.4 to request the auth key needed to register
the device on the H2Train network.
2.5.4 Request an Auth Key
The registration service issues auth keys to authorized users whose institutional
email addresses are included in an approved list (whitelist).

Open the H2Train Tailscale registration page.
Enter your institutional email address in Email address.
Enter a name for the device in Raspberry Pi name, using lowercase letters,
numbers, and hyphens.
Select Request access to begin email verification.

The following example uses jiahao.yang@ulpgc.es and the device name
raspberry-pi-ulpgc-01. Replace these example values with your own email address
and device name.

After submitting the request, continue with email verification in
section 2.5.5.
2.5.5 Verify Your Email Address
The registration service sends a six-digit verification code to the email
address provided, using an external SMTP server. The page then displays the
verification form shown below.


Open your email application and locate the verification message.
If the message is not in your inbox, check the Junk or Spam folder.
Copy the six-digit code from the message.
Return to the registration page, enter the code in Verification code, and
select Verify and get key.

The following screenshot shows an example of the verification email. Use the
code sent to your own email address.

After successful verification, the final step of the registration process
displays the Tailscale auth key and the device registration command, as shown
below. Copy the key or the complete command directly from this page to register
your device.

Use the command displayed in this final step to connect the device as described
in section 2.5.6.
2.5.6 Connect the Device to the Tailscale Network
With Tailscale installed and your auth key available, complete the device
registration:

Copy the device registration command provided by the H2Train registration page.
Paste and run it in the Raspberry Pi terminal. Use the command containing your
newly issued auth key.
Confirm that the device has joined the Tailscale network by running:
tailscale status



This command displays the device's Tailscale connection status and the peers
visible to it on the network.
2.5.7 Request Assistance
If the service cannot issue an auth key, or if your email address is not included
in the whitelist, contact the system administrator at
h2train@proton.me.
Include your institutional email address, the intended device name, and a brief
description of the problem. The administrator will review the request and provide
assistance, including an appropriate auth key once access has been authorized.

chapters/03-installing-eclipse-kura.html.title: 3. Installing Eclipse Kura
chapters/03-installing-eclipse-kura.html.body:
3. Installing Eclipse Kura
This procedure installs Eclipse Kura 5.6.2 and Eclipse Temurin JDK 17 on a
Raspberry Pi using the commands below. Run them in order in a terminal on the
Raspberry Pi, either locally or through SSH.
The Kura package is for 64-bit ARM (aarch64). The Adoptium repository command
uses trixie, so it must match the operating system's Debian release. Confirm
these prerequisites before continuing. You also need internet access, a user
with sudo privileges, and wget available for the download step.
3.1 Update the Operating System
Refresh the list of available packages and versions from the configured repositories.
sudo apt update

Upgrade installed packages to the newer versions available in those repositories.
Confirm the changes when prompted.
sudo apt upgrade

3.2 Download the Kura Installer
Download the Kura 5.6.2 installer for 64-bit ARM and save it in the current directory.
wget http://download.eclipse.org/kura/releases/5.6.2/kura_5.6.2_generic-aarch64_installer.deb

Keep this file in the current directory for the installation step in section 3.4.
3.3 Install JDK 17
Install the download tools (wget and curl), the signing-key tool (gpg), and
trusted certificate authorities (ca-certificates). The -y option automatically
confirms the installation prompt.
sudo apt install -y wget curl gpg ca-certificates

Create the directory where APT will read repository signing keys. The -p option
also creates missing parent directories and accepts an existing directory.
sudo mkdir -p /etc/apt/keyrings

Download Adoptium's public signing key, convert it to the binary format used here,
and save it in the keyring directory. APT uses this key to verify packages from
the Adoptium repository; > /dev/null hides the copy printed by tee.
curl -fsSL https://packages.adoptium.net/artifactory/api/gpg/key/public | gpg --dearmor | sudo tee /etc/apt/keyrings/adoptium.gpg > /dev/null

Allow all users to read the key file, while allowing only its owner to change it.
This lets APT read the signing key.
sudo chmod 644 /etc/apt/keyrings/adoptium.gpg

Add the Adoptium package repository for Debian Trixie to APT's configuration.
The signed-by setting tells APT to verify this repository using the key saved above.
echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/adoptium.gpg] https://packages.adoptium.net/artifactory/deb trixie main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/adoptium.list

Refresh the package list again, this time including the newly added Adoptium repository.
sudo apt update

Install Eclipse Temurin JDK 17, which includes the Java runtime and development
tools. The -y option automatically confirms the installation prompt.
sudo apt install -y temurin-17-jdk

Display the version of the Java runtime selected by the system. Check that it reports
Java 17.
java -version

Display the version of the Java compiler selected by the system. Check that it
also reports version 17. If either check shows another version, resolve the active
Java selection before continuing.
javac -version

3.4 Install Kura and Restart the Device
Install the downloaded Kura package and its dependencies through APT. The ./
prefix tells APT to use the installer file in the current directory.
sudo apt-get install ./kura_5.6.2_generic-aarch64_installer.deb

Restart the Raspberry Pi after the installation finishes successfully. This also
ends the current SSH session; wait for the device to start before reconnecting.
sudo reboot

3.5 Accessing the Administration Interface
After the Raspberry Pi restarts, open the Kura administration console and
complete the initial login setup.
3.5.1 Open the Console
Choose the address according to where you are running the browser:



Browser location
Console address




On the Raspberry Pi itself
https://localhost


On another computer that can reach the Raspberry Pi
https://



Replace  with the Raspberry Pi's IP address. When using another
computer, localhost refers to that computer, so use the Raspberry Pi's address.
3.5.2 Handle the Certificate Warning
The browser may display a certificate warning, as shown below. Kura's default
HTTPS certificate is self-signed, so the browser cannot automatically verify
the device's identity.

For this initial setup, confirm that the address belongs to your Raspberry Pi,
then open Advanced and select Proceed to localhost or the equivalent
option for the device's IP address. The wording may vary between browsers.
3.5.3 Sign In and Change the Password
For a fresh installation, use the default credentials:



Field
Value




Username
admin


Password
admin



Complete the password-change prompt shown during the initial login. If no prompt
appears, use the user menu to select Change password. Set a new password and,
if prompted to sign in again, use the updated credentials.
For further details, consult the official Kura Raspberry Pi quick start
and the Adoptium Linux installation guide.
Console access, default credentials, and certificate warnings are covered in the
Kura administration console guide.

chapters/04-connecting-to-h2train.html.title: 4. Connecting to Cloud Multiplatform H2Train with Eclipse Kapua
chapters/04-connecting-to-h2train.html.body:
4. Connecting to Cloud Multiplatform H2Train with Eclipse Kapua
This chapter describes how to register a Kapua user and configure Eclipse Kura
for device maintenance through Cloud Multiplatform H2Train. Complete the steps
in the order presented, using the connection settings for the deployment
described below.
4.1 Register a Kapua User
Before configuring the device, create a user on the Kapua server through the
Kapua registration page. This application
is hosted on Vercel and uses the Kapua API to create new users.

Open the registration page.
Enter a username and choose a password.
Submit the registration form. The system assigns the user's role automatically.

The following example shows the registration of a user named ulpgc with a
password chosen by the user.

Once registration is complete, confirm in the Kapua administration console that
the user has been created successfully, as illustrated below.

Registration provides each user with individual credentials for broker
authentication. The maintenance connection configured in section 4.5 uses a
dedicated maintenance account with its own roles and permissions.
4.2 Import the SSL Certificate into Kura
Download the SSL certificate provided in the
deployment certificate Gist.
Then import it through the Kura administration console:

Open the Security section.
Select Add, then Certificate.
Select SSLKeystore as the destination keystore.
Select the downloaded certificate file and complete the import.

The certificate is used to establish trust for the secure connection to the broker.
4.3 Create the Maintenance Cloud Connection
In the Kura administration console, open Cloud Connections and select
New Connection. Configure the connection as follows:



Field
Value




Cloud Connection Factory PID
org.eclipse.kura.cloud.CloudService


Cloud Connection Service PID
org.eclipse.kura.cloud.CloudService-Maintainer



Create the connection, then continue with its data service configuration.
4.4 Enable Automatic Connection at Startup
Open the DataService-Maintainer section of the new cloud connection.

Set Connect Auto-on-Startup to true.
Select Apply to save the changes.
Open MqttDataTransport-Maintainer to configure the broker connection.

4.5 Configure the MQTT Transport
Configure MqttDataTransport-Maintainer using the values shown below and in
the accompanying screenshot.



Field
Value




Broker-url
mqtts://10.0.0.20:8883/


Topic Context Account-Name
H2TRAIN


Username
maintenance


Password
1234


Client-id
rpi-kura, or another identifier unique within the account


Keep-alive
30 seconds


Timeout
10 seconds


Clean-session
true




Use the dedicated maintenance account for this connection. Its roles and
permissions are intended for maintenance-related communication. Enter 1234
as the password for the deployment described in this chapter.
The Client-id may be changed to identify the device. Keep all other settings
as shown in the screenshot, then select Apply to save the configuration.
4.6 Configure the Command Service
Select CommandService in the left navigation panel. Configure the service
as shown in the following screenshot, entering 1234 in Command Password Value.



Field
Value




Command Enable
true


Command Password Value
1234


Command Working Directory
/tmp


Command Timeout
360 seconds


Command Environment
Leave empty


Privileged/Unprivileged Command Service Selection
true




Keep the remaining settings as shown and select Apply to save the changes.
4.7 Configuration Outcome
These steps complete the Kura configuration for device maintenance in the
described deployment. User registration provides individual broker credentials,
while the dedicated maintenance cloud connection and Command Service provide
the configuration needed for a Kapua administrator to carry out remote
maintenance operations, including application updates.

chapters/05-glossary-and-references.html.title: 5. Glossary and Reference Material
chapters/05-glossary-and-references.html.body:
5. Glossary and Reference Material
This chapter explains the terminology used in the manual and brings together
the external documentation and deployment resources needed for installation,
network access, and cloud configuration.
5.1 Glossary
The definitions below describe terms in the context of the procedures in
chapters 2 through 4.
5.1.1 Hardware and Operating System



Term
Definition




AArch64 (aarch64)
The 64-bit ARM architecture targeted by the Kura installer used in this manual.


Debian
The Linux distribution on which the Raspberry Pi OS release used in this implementation is based.


GPIO
General-Purpose Input/Output. The Raspberry Pi header used to interface with external electronics; it also includes power pins.


microSD card
Removable storage used here for the operating system, installed software, and device data.


RAM
Random-Access Memory. Working memory used by the operating system and running applications. The device described here has 4 GB.


Raspberry Pi 4 Model B
The single-board computer used as the Kura device in this implementation.


Raspberry Pi OS
The operating system used on the device, previously known as Raspbian. This procedure uses its 64-bit edition.


SoC
System on Chip. An integrated circuit combining the processor and other core hardware functions.


Trixie
The release name for Debian 13, used by the operating system and Adoptium repository configuration in this manual.



5.1.2 Software Installation and Administration



Term
Definition




APT (apt, apt-get)
Debian package-management tools used to refresh package lists, install software, and upgrade installed packages.


curl and wget
Command-line download tools. The procedures use them to retrieve installers, scripts, and a repository signing key.


DEB package (.deb)
A Debian software package. Kura is installed from a local file in this format.


Dependency
Software required by another application, such as the Java runtime needed to run Kura.


Eclipse Temurin
The OpenJDK distribution installed to provide Java 17 in this implementation.


GPG signing key
A cryptographic key used by APT to verify repository signatures and the authenticity of package information.


Java runtime and JDK
The runtime executes Java applications. The Java Development Kit (JDK) includes the runtime and development tools such as the javac compiler.


Package repository
A source of software packages and package information used by APT, such as the Adoptium repository.


Root and sudo
Root is the Linux administrator account. sudo allows an authorized user to run a command with elevated privileges.


SSH
Secure Shell. A protocol used to open an encrypted remote terminal session on the Raspberry Pi.


Working directory
The directory in which a command runs. The Command Service configuration uses /tmp for this purpose.



5.1.3 Networking, Security, and VPN Access



Term
Definition




Auth key
A Tailscale credential used to register a device on a tailnet without an interactive browser login on that device. It is separate from the Kapua broker credentials.


Authentication
Checking the identity of a user or device, for example by validating credentials or an email verification code.


Authorization
Determining which resources or operations an authenticated user or device may access, according to assigned roles and permissions.


Certificate and certificate authority (CA)
A certificate binds an identity to a public key. A CA signs certificates that clients may trust when the issuing CA is trusted.


DNS
Domain Name System. Resolves names, such as a server hostname, to network addresses.


HTTPS
HTTP protected by TLS. It is used to access the Kura console and registration websites through an encrypted connection.


IP address and port
An IP address identifies a network interface; a port identifies a service endpoint at that address. The broker example uses port 8883.


localhost
A name referring to the computer on which the browser or command is running. It identifies the Raspberry Pi only when used on that device.


Self-signed certificate
A certificate signed by its own key rather than by an external CA. Kura's default certificate can therefore produce a browser trust warning.


SMTP
Simple Mail Transfer Protocol. Used by the registration service's external mail server to send verification messages.


SSL and TLS
SSL is the older protocol name still present in some interface labels. TLS is the protocol used to protect current HTTPS and secure MQTT connections.


SSLKeystore
The Kura keystore selected when importing the broker certificate in chapter 4. It stores certificate material used for secure connections.


Tailscale and tailnet
Tailscale provides the private network used in the temporary deployment. A tailnet is the Tailscale network to which authorized devices connect.


Verification code
The six-digit code emailed during VPN registration to confirm access to the supplied email address. It is separate from the auth key issued afterward.


VPN
Virtual Private Network. Provides private connectivity between devices across different networks or geographical locations.


Whitelist (allowlist)
The approved list of institutional email addresses permitted to request Tailscale access through the H2Train registration service.



For installation and auth key details, see the Tailscale resources in
section 5.2.3.
5.1.4 Eclipse Kura, Eclipse Kapua, and Messaging



Term
Definition




API
Application Programming Interface. Allows one application to interact with another; the Kapua registration page uses the Kapua API to create users.


Broker
The MQTT server that receives published messages and forwards them to clients subscribed to the corresponding topics.


Clean session
An MQTT option controlling session state. With true, the connection starts a new session and does not preserve its session state after disconnection.


Client ID
The identifier representing a device's MQTT client. It must be unique within the account used by this deployment.


Cloud connection
The configured group of Kura services used to communicate with a cloud platform. This manual creates a dedicated maintenance connection.


CloudService
The Kura service providing cloud messaging and management functions above the data service and transport layers.


CommandService
The Kura service configured to receive and execute remote commands for maintenance operations.


DataService
The Kura service responsible for managing message delivery above the transport layer. Its startup option controls automatic connection in this procedure.


Eclipse Kapua
The cloud platform used here to manage connected devices, user access, and device communication.


Eclipse Kura
The software framework installed on the Raspberry Pi to configure the gateway and connect it to cloud services.


Edge device and gateway
An edge device operates close to local equipment or data sources. A gateway connects those devices or applications to other systems; the Raspberry Pi running Kura serves this role.


H2Train
The project platform referred to as Cloud Multiplatform H2Train in this manual. The documented setup uses Kapua for device maintenance.


IoT
Internet of Things. Connected physical devices that exchange data and can be monitored or managed through software services.


Keep-alive
The MQTT interval used to check that a connection remains active. The client sends a ping when needed during periods without other traffic.


MQTT and MQTTS
MQTT is a publish/subscribe messaging protocol. The mqtts:// scheme in the broker URL indicates MQTT protected by TLS.


MqttDataTransport
The Kura transport service that connects to the MQTT broker using the configured address, credentials, and client ID.


PID and factory PID
A Persistent Identifier identifies a service configuration in Kura. A factory PID identifies the factory used to create service instances; a service PID identifies the configured instance.


Timeout
The time limit for an operation. MQTT transport and Command Service timeouts apply to different operations and are configured separately.


Topic
The name used to route published MQTT messages to interested subscribers.


Topic Context Account-Name
The account name Kura inserts into its topic namespace. The documented configuration uses H2TRAIN; this value is distinct from the broker username.



The Kura cloud connection guide
and MQTT transport configuration reference
provide further details about these services and settings.
5.2 External References and Useful Resources
The following resources support the procedures in this manual. Use the Kura
5.6 documentation for the installation described here. Generic examples in
upstream guides may use different server addresses, accounts, or credentials;
use the deployment-specific settings in chapter 4 for H2Train.
5.2.1 Raspberry Pi Hardware and Operating System



Resource
Purpose




Raspberry Pi 4 Model B
Hardware specifications, interfaces, and power requirements for the device used in chapter 2.


Raspberry Pi OS downloads
Official operating system images and information about their architecture and Debian base.



5.2.2 Eclipse Kura, Eclipse Kapua, and Java



Resource
Purpose




Eclipse Kura documentation
General documentation entry point and access to other Kura documentation versions.


Eclipse Kura 5.6 documentation
Documentation for the release series used in this manual.


Install Kura
Installation profiles, package selection, and runtime requirements.


Raspberry Pi quick start
Kura installation guidance for Raspberry Pi OS.


Kura 5.6.2 ARM64 installer
The installer file downloaded in section 3.2.


Gateway Administration Console
Console access, initial credentials, password changes, and HTTPS certificate warnings.


Cloud Connections
Creating and managing Kura cloud connections.


Data Transport Service Configuration
MQTT broker settings, client identity, sessions, and connection timeouts.


Eclipse Kapua repository
Project documentation, source code, and deployment guides.


Kura-to-Kapua connection guide
An upstream connection example to complement the H2Train procedure.


Adoptium Linux installation guide
Configuring the Temurin package repository and installing the required JDK.



5.2.3 Tailscale



Resource
Purpose




Install Tailscale on Linux
Official Linux installation instructions and connection checks.


Tailscale installation script
